title: Brocard–Ramanujan factorial squares
summary: The numbers 4! + 1, 5! + 1, and 7! + 1 are squares. Do these examples exhaust all natural numbers n for which n! + 1 is a square?

tasks.title: Check the initial factorials
tasks.context: Evaluate n! + 1 for n=0 through 7. The values 25, 121 and 5041 are the three exact squares. Put each other value strictly between consecutive squares and use monotonicity on the naturals.

tasks.title: Factor a hypothetical larger factorial
tasks.claim:
∀ n m : ℕ, 8 ≤ n → Nat.factorial n + 1 = m ^ 2 →
    ∃ a : ℕ, Nat.factorial n = 4 * (a * (a + 1))
tasks.role: Turns the square equation into a product of consecutive factors.
tasks.context: For n≥8 the factorial is even, so m is odd. Write m=2a+1 and expand m²−1=4a(a+1). This formulation is equivalent to the square equation in the larger range.

tasks.title: Exclude the remaining consecutive factorizations
tasks.claim: ∀ n a : ℕ, 8 ≤ n → Nat.factorial n ≠ 4 * (a * (a + 1))
tasks.role: Would rule out a fourth pair.
tasks.context: This is the open step. Since a and a+1 are coprime, each prime-power block of n!/4 lies entirely on one side. Try to rule out partitions into consecutive products. A modular sieve can rule out ranges but does not give an unbounded proof on its own. See Berndt and Galway (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009873805276) for the bounded sieve approach.
